strengths: Significance: Efficient causal discovery at hundreds or thousands of variables is an important problem, and the reported sub-second inference at 1,000 nodes would be practically valuable if validated.

Soundness merits: The two-stream architecture, progressive sample-axis reduction, and tied axial attention form a coherent efficiency-oriented design. The paper provides useful ablations of reduction, graph priors, graph streams, attention, prediction heads, and pooling strategies.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover several graph families, linear and nonlinear mechanisms, distribution shifts, a semi-synthetic gene-regulatory simulator, multiple accuracy metrics, and diverse baselines.

Presentation and ethics: The overall architecture and tensor shapes are explained reasonably clearly. The impact statement appropriately warns that predicted graphs are hypotheses sensitive to data quality, assumptions, and distribution shift and should be independently validated.
weaknesses: Soundness: The graph prior is defined as the inverse of the empirical covariance, but the principal 1,000-node experiment has only 1,000 samples. After centering, this covariance has rank at most 999 and is necessarily singular. No pseudoinverse, ridge regularization, numerical stabilization, or ablation is specified, making a central reported result mathematically underspecified and difficult to reproduce.

Soundness/fairness: CauScale receives an intervention indicator for every sample, while the data contain a mixture of observational and single-node-interventional regimes. The paper does not explain how observational methods such as standard NOTEARS, FCI, DiffAN, and SDCD are adapted to these regimes; naively pooling them violates their single-distribution assumptions. Thus the large performance advantage may partly reflect privileged intervention information and an invalid baseline protocol.

The AVICI comparison is also confounded: CauScale is trained on the paper's graph and mechanism distributions, whereas AVICI uses externally pretrained checkpoints because retraining caused OOM. This does not isolate architectural quality or scalability under matched training data and compute.

Evidence is too limited for the magnitude of the claims. Each test configuration uses only five graph instances, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The main benchmarks remain synthetic or semi-synthetic and largely use the same generators and intervention design as training; no real dataset or established real-data benchmark supports the scientific-use claims.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the training loss is never defined, the advertised project-page URL is blank, and code is not supplied. Seeds, precise train/validation/test splitting, checkpoint selection, inverse-covariance handling, intervention allocation, and several implementation choices needed to reproduce the results are missing.

The efficiency analysis covers only data-stream attention and omits the graph stream, which operates on an n-by-n representation and can incur cubic computation, as well as the cost of constructing the inverse-covariance prior. It is unclear whether preprocessing is included in timing. The main memory claim is supported chiefly by OOM statements and a small-scale ablation rather than controlled numerical memory measurements across the claimed scales.

The model does not enforce acyclicity. Its three-way pairwise head prevents opposite edges within a pair but cannot prevent longer directed cycles. Cycle measurements are only shown for a restricted small-scale ablation, with no large-scale DAG-validity results or post-processing, despite the paper framing the output as causal DAG discovery.

Originality is moderate: tied attention is adopted from Rao et al., the prediction head from Lippe et al., and average-pooling reduction is conceptually simple. Their combination may be useful, but the paper does not clearly establish a new causal-learning principle beyond this engineering synthesis.

Presentation has several unresolved inconsistencies and ambiguities, including the claim of a sixfold tied-attention speedup despite Figure 5 showing roughly a 2–3-fold difference, unclear decoding details for SHD, and no test of sensitivity to the arbitrary ordering/grouping of samples introduced by chunked pooling. Collectively, these technical and evidential gaps prevent the central superiority and scalability claims from being considered reliable.

strengths: The engineering goal is important: amortized causal discovery at larger graph sizes could be useful, and combining progressive sample reduction, tied axial attention, and a graph stream is coherent.

The evaluation covers several graph sizes and mechanisms, reports multiple structural metrics and runtime, and includes both synthetic SCMs and the SERGIO semi-synthetic simulator. Some reported improvements are substantial, particularly on in-distribution synthetic data.
The paper provides asymptotic efficiency analysis and ablations of the reduction unit, graph prior/stream, attention mechanism, prediction head, and pooling strategy.

The manuscript is generally readable, with useful architecture diagrams. Its impact statement appropriately warns that predicted graphs should be treated as hypotheses requiring expert or experimental validation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The baseline comparison appears fundamentally unfair. CauScale explicitly receives intervention indicators, whereas several baselines as configured—FCI, NOTEARS, SDCD, and DiffAN—do not use intervention targets and generally assume a single observational distribution. Pooling heterogeneous intervention regimes can violate their assumptions. Without observational-only experiments or intervention-aware baselines, the large accuracy gains do not reliably establish method superiority.

Soundness: The graph prior is defined as the unregularized inverse empirical covariance. For the headline 1000-node/1000-sample experiment, centering limits covariance rank to at most 999, making it singular. No pseudoinverse, shrinkage, jitter, or other numerical treatment is documented, leaving a central model input undefined as written.

Soundness: Independent three-state predictions for node pairs prevent two-cycles but not longer directed cycles. The paper neither enforces acyclicity nor reports DAG validity on the main 1000-node and SERGIO experiments. The small ablation's undefined “Cycles” percentage is insufficient.

Soundness: Chunking consecutive observations and pooling within chunks may make predictions depend on the arbitrary ordering of i.i.d. samples. The paper gives neither a permutation-invariance argument nor an empirical permutation-robustness test.

Evidence and significance: The abstract's 84.4% OOD mAP is selective—it is the 100-node sigmoid result. CauScale obtains only 18.9 mAP on the 1000-node polynomial setting, below SDCD at 29.8 and SEA at 20.6. Its 100-node polynomial result is 50.3. The broad OOD claims are therefore overstated.

Evidence: Each test configuration contains only five graph instances, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The tuning and validation splits are unspecified, so the reliability of near-perfect scores and method rankings cannot be assessed.

Evidence: SERGIO is still a simulator, and the evaluation uses graph families and mechanisms closely related to training. There is no genuine empirical dataset, biological validation, or standard real causal benchmark supporting the claimed practical scientific utility.

Efficiency: Runtime comparisons omit the roughly 40 hours of eight-H200 training needed for amortization and do not adequately specify device allocation, warm-up, preprocessing, batching, or variance. Main-table peak-memory results are absent despite memory scalability being a central claim. Training at 500 nodes with batch size one on a 141-GB H200 is also limited evidence of accessibility.

Originality is moderate. Tied attention is adopted from prior work, average pooling is standard, and pairwise prediction follows Lippe et al. The two-stream synthesis may be useful, but the paper provides little new causal insight, no identifiability result, and insufficient evidence isolating architectural novelty from intervention supervision and training scale.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-page URL is blank, code and checkpoints are unavailable, and the training objective is not stated. Covariance regularization, CauScale decoding thresholds, data splits, random seeds, intervention allocation, detailed graph parameters, timing protocol, and full hyperparameter selection are also missing.

Presentation contains consequential imprecision: mAP and orientation-accuracy aggregation are vague, the cycle statistic is undefined, and the text calls CauScale the fastest evaluated method even though CORR and INVCOV are faster in the table. Several typos and overly strong interpretations further hinder auditing.

Ethics and limitations: There is no obvious unresolved ethical violation, and the impact statement is appropriately cautious. However, the limitations discussion omits the intervention-information mismatch, simulator dependence, lack of acyclicity, weak large-scale polynomial OOD performance, extreme hardware requirements, and ambiguity of the inverse-covariance prior. Overall, the promising engineering and strong reported numbers are outweighed by major soundness, evaluation, and reproducibility problems.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated and generally well organized, with helpful architecture diagrams, complexity discussion, and appendices describing data generation and baseline implementations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/46ce9ca4d52143dcb1ababeef9d88282/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported empirical gains are substantial: CauScale achieves strong accuracy on synthetic and SERGIO benchmarks while being much faster than optimization-based methods, including 0.83-second inference for the reported 1000-node setting.

The reduction unit, tied attention, and data/graph streams form a practically useful design. Ablations separately examine reduction, the graph stream and prior, attention type, prediction head, and pooling strategy.

Evaluation includes multiple graph sizes, nonlinear mechanisms, OOD mechanisms, different noise distributions, and a semi-synthetic gene-regulation simulator. Generalization from graphs of at most 500 nodes to 1000 nodes is promising.

The contribution has meaningful potential significance because scalable amortized causal discovery remains important and difficult. The particular combination is moderately original even though pooling, tied attention, and graph priors are individually established techniques.
The impact statement appropriately warns about distribution shift, spurious edges, and the need for expert or experimental validation before high-stakes use.
weaknesses: A central technical specification appears invalid as written: the graph prior is the unregularized inverse empirical covariance, yet the headline 1000-node experiment uses only 1000 samples. After centering, that covariance has rank at most 999 and is singular. The paper does not state whether it uses a pseudoinverse, shrinkage, or another regularizer, so the reported flagship setting cannot be reproduced from the described method.

The evidence is too narrow for the broad causal-discovery claims. Every main evaluation supplies intervention indicators and apparently includes interventions covering all nodes; SERGIO uses only knockout data. There is no observational-only experiment, limited-intervention study, or evaluation on genuinely measured real-world data. Near-perfect performance under comprehensive simulated interventions therefore does not establish similarly strong general causal discovery.

Results use only five test graphs per configuration and report means without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several major conclusions, including OOD generalization, are presented through plots without uncertainty or exact values, making robustness difficult to judge.

The scalability and memory claims are incompletely substantiated. The paper reports no absolute peak-memory comparison for the main 500- or 1000-node settings, and the memory ablation stops at 100 nodes. AVICI is evaluated from pretrained checkpoints after its retraining reportedly failed, whereas CauScale and SEA receive task-specific training; this complicates both accuracy and resource comparisons. Training also requires eight H200 GPUs, which weakens the claim of computational accessibility.

The efficiency analysis covers only data-stream attention and omits the graph stream operating on an n-by-n representation, whose axial-attention computation can dominate at large n. Consequently, the theoretical analysis does not establish end-to-end scaling in graph size.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the training loss is never defined; code is not supplied and the project-page URL is blank; seeds, validation and checkpoint-selection procedures, intervention sample allocation, covariance stabilization, FFN widths, dropout, and several simulator or graph-generation parameters are missing. Hyperparameter tuning is mentioned without explaining the validation protocol.

The output head predicts each unordered pair independently and does not enforce acyclicity. Although low cycle rates are reported in a restricted ablation, cycle statistics are absent for the main 500- and 1000-node evaluations, so it is unclear whether the principal outputs are valid causal DAGs.

Originality is useful but incremental: the major efficiency ingredients are embedding pooling and tied attention adopted from prior work, while the two-stream fusion resembles established architectural patterns. Given the unresolved specification and evidential issues, the promising empirical contribution is not yet reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: amortized causal discovery for graphs substantially larger than those typically handled by neural approaches. Inference below one second for 1,000-node synthetic graphs, if validated, would be useful.

The architecture combines hierarchical reduction, a graph stream, and tied axial attention in a coherent design. The component and pooling ablations provide some evidence that reduction and the graph stream contribute beyond the base architecture.

The evaluation covers multiple graph sizes, mechanisms, noise distributions, latent-variable stress tests, cyclicity, and several structure and causal-effect metrics. Reporting standard deviations for the main model and discussing failures on polynomial mechanisms are positive practices.

The manuscript is generally readable, includes computational analyses, and gives an appropriate impact statement warning that discovered graphs are hypotheses requiring expert or experimental validation.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility are undermined by a fundamental inconsistency in the graph prior. With D declared as m-by-n, the displayed expression (D-mu)(D-mu)^T is m-by-m, not the claimed n-by-n inverse covariance. Moreover, an ordinary empirical covariance is singular in the n=m=1,000 experiment after centering (rank at most 999). The paper specifies neither a transpose correction nor regularization/pseudoinversion, so a central model input cannot be reproduced as written.

The headline accuracy comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. CauScale receives intervention indicators and is trained on the authors' simulator distributions, while several classical baselines do not naturally exploit the same interventional information and AVICI is evaluated from externally supplied checkpoints. The manuscript does not isolate gains from architecture, training-data match, supervision scale, and access to interventions.

Only five test graphs are used per setting. The resulting uncertainty is large in important cases—for example, 1,000-node polynomial mAP is 18.9±13.8 and SHD is 3985±2975—yet broad superiority and generalization claims are made. Baseline uncertainty is omitted from the main table, preventing statistical comparison.

The abstract's claim of 84.4% mAP on out-of-distribution data selectively reflects the 100-node sigmoid case; OOD polynomial performance is 50.3% at 100 nodes and 18.9% at 1,000 nodes. Thus the headline materially overstates robustness under the paper's own OOD conditions.

The scalability evidence is incomplete. The only quantitative memory ablation is limited to at most 100 nodes, no peak-memory table is provided for the claimed 500-node training or 1,000-node inference regimes, and the memory proposition concerns inference rather than the training bottleneck emphasized in the paper. Comparisons also rely on a single H200-class hardware environment without a careful common-resource protocol.

The method description omits implementation-critical details, including how the inverse covariance is stabilized, loss definition and weighting, FFN widths, dropout, precise intervention sampling counts, and training stopping/checkpoint selection. The project-page URL in the manuscript is blank, so code and configurations are unavailable.

Originality is moderate rather than high: tied attention is adopted from prior work, the reduction unit is repeated average pooling, and the prediction head is adopted from SEA. The two-stream assembly is useful, but the paper does not establish a substantial new causal-discovery principle or theoretical guarantee.

The empirical scope is restricted to synthetic and simulator-generated data. The paper honestly acknowledges the absence of real observational evaluation, but this substantially limits evidence for scientific applicability, particularly given sensitivity to mechanism/noise shift and the assumed causal sufficiency.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in amortized causal discovery and proposes a coherent architecture combining progressive sample-axis reduction, tied axial attention, a graph stream, and a pairwise prediction head.

The empirical results are promising within the simulated regimes: CauScale substantially outperforms the reported baselines on most synthetic and SERGIO settings, evaluates graphs up to 1,000 nodes, and reports several complementary metrics, including SHD, mAP, AUC, orientation accuracy, cyclicity, and AID.

The ablations examine the reduction unit, graph stream, graph prior, attention mechanism, prediction head, and pooling choice. The paper also tests shifts in graph topology, mechanism, noise, sample size, and hidden-node count rather than reporting only in-distribution accuracy.

The architecture and principal computational ideas are presented clearly, with useful diagrams and a FLOP/memory analysis. The limitations and impact discussion appropriately warns that predictions are hypotheses, acknowledges simulator dependence and distribution shift, and raises no material ethical concern. weaknesses: Soundness: the graph prior is defined as the inverse empirical covariance, but central experiments use n=m=1,000. After centering, that covariance has rank at most 999 and therefore cannot be inverted. Table 4 even computes a 1,000-dimensional prior from as few as 10–500 samples. No pseudoinverse, shrinkage, ridge parameter, or numerical procedure is specified, so a central model input is mathematically undefined in key experiments and the reported results cannot presently be reproduced.

Soundness: the evidence does not justify broad causal-discovery claims. Almost all evaluation is on synthetic or semi-synthetic data generated from closely related simulator families, with only five test graphs per setting. The striking pure-observational orientation results are not accompanied by an identifiability argument explaining which simulator asymmetries permit recovery; they may reflect learned generator-specific regularities rather than transferable causal information. No real observational benchmark is evaluated.

The latent-confounder analysis is conceptually weak: it hides high-out-degree nodes but scores against the induced observable sub-DAG. Marginalizing hidden common causes generally induces a latent projection/ADMG rather than merely deleting those nodes. This experiment therefore does not establish valid causal discovery under latent confounding, despite being described as robustness to latent confounders.

The efficiency comparison is incomplete and potentially misleading. It contrasts zero-shot inference with per-dataset optimization while omitting CauScale's substantial pretraining cost (roughly 318 GPU-hours for the stated synthetic stages), does not clearly state which baselines run on CPU versus GPU, gives no timing variance or measurement protocol, and provides no main quantitative memory table. Thus the headline 4×–13,000× speedup is not a sufficient end-to-end efficiency comparison.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript does not specify the training loss, FFN width, dropout and regularization settings, exact edge-weight distributions and DAG-orientation procedure, prior stabilization, decoding threshold, random seeds, or complete hyperparameter-selection protocol. The project-page link is blank, and no code or trained models are provided. The highly consequential cycle-breaking and inverse-covariance computations also lack implementation detail.

Several evaluation choices weaken fairness: CORR and INVCOV are thresholded using the ground-truth edge count, other baselines use disparate fixed thresholds, AVICI uses pretrained checkpoints rather than matched training while CauScale and some SEA variants receive the authors' training distribution, and uncertainty for the main baseline comparisons is omitted. Five graphs, coupled with very large CauScale standard deviations in some n=1,000 settings, are insufficient for strong superiority claims.

Originality is moderate rather than high. Progressive average pooling, tied attention imported from prior work, inverse-covariance features, and a two-stream fusion design form a useful engineering combination, but the manuscript provides limited new causal insight or theoretical justification for why information discarded by pooling preserves causal evidence. The ablation without reduction also changes the feasible training distribution, so it does not cleanly isolate the reduction unit's accuracy effect.

Presentation is generally readable, but some claims overreach the evidence—for example, “without sacrificing discovery quality,” robustness to confounding, and broad scalability—while the polynomial OOD result at n=1,000 is poor and unstable (18.9±13.8 mAP; 3,985±2,975 SHD). Overall, the undefined prior and insufficiently reproducible, simulator-bound validation are important technical and evidential deficiencies that prevent acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The core efficiency result is convincing within the evaluated synthetic setting. CauScale processes 1,000-node graphs in 0.83 seconds and substantially outperforms the tested baselines on most synthetic and SERGIO metrics; component ablations support the contributions of reduction, tied attention, the graph stream, and the graph prior.

Significance: Scaling amortized causal discovery to training graphs with 500 nodes and inference graphs with 1,000 nodes is useful. The reported speed and memory improvements could enable substantially larger simulation studies and rapid hypothesis generation.

Originality: The individual ingredients are not new, but their combination—progressive sample-axis compression, tied axial attention, and a data/graph two-stream architecture—is a sensible and practically effective system contribution.

Evaluation: The paper covers multiple graph sizes, causal mechanisms, noise distributions, graph families, sample sizes, pooling choices, and limited latent-variable stress tests. It also reports SHD, mAP, AUC, orientation accuracy, cyclicity, AID, runtime, memory, and standard deviations for CauScale.

Presentation: The architecture and its computational motivation are generally clear, and the FLOP and activation-memory analyses are helpful. Figures 1–5 communicate the design and ablations effectively.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript appropriately acknowledges reliance on simulated data and warns that learned graphs require expert or experimental validation before high-stakes use. No unresolved ethical concern is apparent. weaknesses: Soundness: The graph prior is defined as an ordinary inverse covariance matrix, but the centered covariance is necessarily singular when n=1,000 and m=1,000. No regularization, pseudoinverse, or treatment of mixed observational/interventional regimes is specified. This is an important methodological and reproducibility omission.

The evidence remains almost entirely synthetic: SERGIO is itself a simulator, and the observational-only appendix has no baseline comparison. Near-perfect orientation on observational linear-Gaussian data should be framed as meta-distribution performance rather than generic causal identifiability; it can arise from learned simulator priors that need not transfer to real data.

Baseline comparability is imperfect. CauScale is trained on the authors’ generators, whereas AVICI uses released checkpoints, some classical baselines use default hyperparameters, and only SEA is retrained on matched data in some settings. The headline speedups compare amortized inference—after roughly 320 H200 GPU-hours of training—with per-dataset optimization while omitting amortized training cost.

Only five test graphs are used per configuration. CauScale has very large variability in difficult settings, such as 18.9±13.8 mAP and 3985±2975 SHD for the 1,000-node polynomial case, while uncertainty is not reported for most baseline results. This weakens claims of consistent superiority.

The latent-confounder experiment evaluates against the induced observable sub-DAG after deleting hidden common causes. Marginalizing such causes generally produces latent-variable structure rather than merely that sub-DAG, so this experiment does not establish robustness to latent confounding in the usual causal-discovery sense.

The abstract’s 84.4% OOD figure is selective: performance falls to 50.3% on the 100-node polynomial mechanism and 18.9% on the combined 1,000-node/polynomial shift. Generalization claims should distinguish single-axis from compounded distribution shifts.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project-page URL is blank, code and checkpoints are not provided in the manuscript, several simulator and evaluation choices are underspecified, and reproducing training requires unusually large hardware. The exact graph-decoding thresholds and timing protocol also deserve a consolidated description.

Presentation has minor but noticeable issues, including grammatical errors, inconsistent terminology, a Figure 7/Table 7 mismatch, and dense tables. The work is a promising weak accept, but stronger real-data validation and a more controlled matched-training comparison would be needed for a confident accept.
